For $R>4$, the partial-fraction identity gives

$$\int_4^R\frac{7}{2x^2-5x-3}\,dx=\int_4^R\frac{dx}{x-3}-2\int_4^R\frac{dx}{2x+1}.$$

Both terms have the same finite upper bound. Integrating and combining the logarithms before taking a limit yields

$$\begin{aligned}
\int_4^R\frac{7}{2x^2-5x-3}\,dx
&=\left[\ln(x-3)-\ln(2x+1)\right]_4^R\\
&=\ln\frac{R-3}{2R+1}+\ln9
=\ln\frac{9(R-3)}{2R+1}.
\end{aligned}$$

Therefore,

$$\int_4^\infty\frac{7}{2x^2-5x-3}\,dx
=\lim_{R\to\infty}\ln\frac{9(R-3)}{2R+1}
=\ln\frac92.$$

The limit is finite, so the improper integral converges. The two partial-fraction improper integrals each diverge when considered separately; keeping a common finite upper bound avoids an undefined subtraction.
